patients.label: Three-day-old male neonate with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

identity_evidence.quote: a rare case of the condition occurring in a three-day-old neonate

attribution_limitations: Electrolytes are reported normal during the initial workup, yet the Discussion later cites normalization of hydration and electrolyte levels after surgery.

The source says "the surgery" and "postoperatively" without naming whether this is the exploratory laparotomy, the pyloromyotomy or one operation comprising both; it also does not state that the pyloromyotomy was performed on day 7 or that the laparotomy preceded the pyloromyotomy.
The mother is described as having an otherwise unremarkable medical history without naming any condition.
The Discharge outcome merges the Results statement of discharge timing with the Discussion statement of discharge in stable condition; both describe the single discharge of this neonate.

evidence.quote:
Figure 1
Abdominal X-ray showing abnormal bowel gas patternThe orange arrow points to the prominent gastric gas bubble (dilated stomach), and the blue arrow points to an area of the abdomen with paucity of distal bowel gas

Figure 2
Delayed gastric emptying and intermittent threadlike passage of the contrast at the antral levelThe blue arrow points to the large, contrast-filled structure in the left upper abdomen. This is indeed the distended stomach, which is the expected appearance in pyloric obstruction. The orange arrow points to a very thin, trickling column of contrast at the gastric outlet. This matches what is typically described as the “string sign,” representing contrast passing through a narrowed pyloric canal. The purple arrow points just distal to the pylorus, where almost no contrast is visible, consistent with paucity of contrast beyond the pylorus, a hallmark of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis

Figure 3
Ultrasonography showed a canal length of 17.2 mm

Figure 4
Ultrasonography showing a pyloric muscle thickness of 4.8 mm

claims.text: A male neonate born at 36 weeks of gestation by C-section for placenta previa, weighing 2,970 g, had an uncomplicated delivery and routine nursery care. He passed urine and meconium within the first 24 hours and had regurgitations since birth. Persistent nonbilious emesis began on day 3 of life with mild abdominal distension, normal bowel sounds and no palpable mass.
